coldOpen.text: This is an options trading bot that ran on a schedule against a one hundred thousand dollar Alpaca paper account. A language model suggests trades. It is never allowed to place one. A deterministic core checks every suggestion against a fixed list of risk gates, and only what the core approves reaches the broker. Every step is written down in public before it happens.

dashboardOpen.text: No login, no export, no screenshot of a spreadsheet. This is the public dashboard on its pinned address, frozen at the presentation cutoff, so a judge sees the same numbers the builder does. The top of the page shows equity, profit and loss against the broker recorded start, and whether the book is flat. It is flat. Everything below it is folded from the journal.

decisionCycle.text: Here is one cycle, in order. Phase zero reconciles the journal against the broker: every position and order must match something the agent wrote down, and anything foreign halts new entries. Phase one takes a fresh account snapshot and fresh quotes. Then the analyst runs. That is Claude, in a child process with read-only market data credentials, reading Alpaca through the MCP server: assets, stock data, options data. It cannot see the account, positions or orders. What comes back is a list of candidate structures in a fixed schema.

gateVector.text: The core prices every candidate from its own quotes, not the analyst's. Then eight gates run in a fixed order. Defined risk first: if maximum loss is not fixed at entry, the candidate dies there. Then sleeve budget, max loss per position, concentration, liquidity, session, idempotency, schema and whitelist. In cycle two, a SPY credit spread failed gate five, liquidity: one leg's quote size was below the minimum. Vetoed, reason recorded.

orderToOutcome.text: An approved plan becomes a multi-leg limit order, revalidated against fresh broker truth, then sent to the Alpaca REST API under a client order id. Intent is journaled before, outcome after. Intent eight: one SPY put credit spread, filled at one dollar six, three hundred ninety-five dollars of max loss reserved. Closed by the deadline route at fifty-eight cents. Forty-eight dollars realized.

architecture.text: Two earlier bots of mine died on economics, not on bugs: TradeScan-AI's predicted edge on a cTrader FIX feed was smaller than retail costs, and Vigil's market making on OKX sat below the fee floor. So this build inverts the shape. The model is not asked to predict. It proposes, inside a whitelist of underlyings, structures and expiries. The strategy is a declared barbell, reserve, income sleeve, convex sleeve, not a forecast. And the boundary is enforced in continuous integration: the pure core cannot import anything that does input or output, and it cannot read the clock.

pnlAndLimits.text: Five hundred eighty-three dollars, fifty-eight basis points. One four-contract QQQ call caught an overnight gap. That single trade is sixty-one percent of the result. Peak fixed worst case was three thousand four hundred twenty-one dollars; the difference between that and what came back is path, not skill. On the last day, two things broke. The runner could not price the next session's expiries, so three closes never went out. The dead-man watchdog had been inert for a day, killed by its own wrapper. Fixed an hour before it was needed, it closed three structures. Two sessions of paper trading prove nothing about edge. No alpha is claimed.

sourceAndTests.text: The repository is public under MIT: the pure core, its tests, the decision log and these build rules. The journal holds every candidate, every gate verdict and every broker order id. One test drives the ugly path, a journal failure with exposure open, and asserts that the agent reduces risk and records the audit gap. The pinned route stays addressable by journal revision and cutoff.
